title: Cloud and DevOps InfoQ Trends Report 2026: AI, Resilience, Platforms, FinOps, and Sovereignty
gist: An InfoQ practitioner panel (Daniel Bryant hosting Matt Saunders, Mark Silvester, Shweta Vohra, Renato Losio and Steef-Jan Wiggers) names AI infrastructure build-out — ~$450bn through 2025 plus 2026 deals like SpaceX+Anthropic and SpaceX+Google — as the biggest surprise of the year, alongside the collapse in major-cloud reliability (an AWS region offline six months, US-East Virginia down last October). The sharpest practitioner signals: AI shifted from encouraged experiment to board-level mandate exposing unprepared teams, no FinOps tool ties token spend to outcomes, Bedrock-style managed AI layers are seen as an onboarding step rather than durable architecture, and half of one European consultancy's clients are migrating back on-prem.

themes.theme: AI capex and the energy bill behind it

insights.claim: AI infrastructure spending is the largest build-out in technology history, running around $450 billion through 2025, with the electricity burned alongside the chips being the genuinely shocking component rather than the chips or agents themselves.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Anchors the AI capex cycle at a scale that makes power generation and grid capacity, not chip supply, the binding second-order constraint to track.
insights.quote: what surprised me the most is not AI chips, not the agents, but the AI infrastructure spending is the largest build-out in the technology world ever
insights.locator: What cloud and DevOps trends surprised the panel most?

insights.claim: 2026 AI infrastructure deals including SpaceX plus Anthropic and SpaceX plus Google, alongside continued heavy AWS and Microsoft spend, mark an escalation beyond the prior year's already-large build-out.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Non-traditional infrastructure partners entering AI compute deals signals the capex frontier is moving beyond terrestrial data centers — a new axis of competition to monitor.
insights.locator: Because if you have heard about SpaceX plus Anthropic

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are in an agent infrastructure arms race, shipping agent registries, DevOps agents at AWS and Microsoft, Google's GKE Agent Sandbox, Cloudflare dynamic workloads and Microsoft's Foundry-based governance layer — a reversal from a year earlier when AI was still the unaddressed elephant in the room.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Agent infrastructure has become a shipped-product battleground across all four major clouds within twelve months — feature parity will arrive fast and differentiation must shift to governance.
insights.quote: I would say the agent infrastructure arms race basically going on.
insights.locator: What cloud and DevOps trends surprised the panel most?

insights.claim: AI has moved within one year from something teams were encouraged to experiment with to an absolute must at leadership and board level, which exposes teams that are not organizationally set up for it.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Board mandate without organizational readiness is the classic precondition for wasted spend — expect a wave of AI project write-offs and remediation consulting.
insights.quote: how fast it's gone from AI being something that teams were encouraged to experiment with, create something that's more efficient, to it being an absolute must from leadership level and the board
insights.locator: Mark, can I throw it over to you? What surprised you

insights.claim: The AI software-delivery community has split into two camps — one betting on ever bigger, faster frontier models to absorb ever larger problems, the other composing smaller specialized agents (coding, testing, CI) with microservices-style thinking — and whether they reconverge or one proves to be hype is the key open question.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: The bigger-model vs. composed-agents split determines whether value accrues to model labs or to orchestration and infrastructure vendors — the central allocation question in AI dev tooling.
insights.locator: Matt, wrapping us up for what surprise

insights.claim: Major cloud reliability was surprisingly poor over the past year, including an AWS region offline for six months due to a war or similar event and US Virginia down for a substantial period last October with repercussions across half the internet — outcomes the panel says would have been unforecastable a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Undercuts the implicit reliability premium in hyperscaler pricing and strengthens the multi-region, multi-cloud and geopolitical-risk case for architecture spend.
insights.quote: what really surprised me is how poor reliability of the major cloud services have been the last year
insights.locator: Let me throw it over to Renato. What's your thoughts on surprises

insights.claim: The reliability degradation is attributed to the pressure of new servers and new AI workloads on cloud capacity rather than to random misfortune.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: If AI demand is degrading baseline cloud reliability, expect continued outage frequency as inference load grows — a systematic rather than transient risk to cloud-dependent businesses.
insights.locator: If someone had told me one year ago that we'll see this kind of number

themes.theme: Governance is the enterprise AI bottleneck

insights.claim: Enterprise AI adoption in regulated environments is being blocked by a coordination failure where team A ships something while team B is already 50% through building something very similar, wasting substantial effort because knowledge is not shared across the organization.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Duplication, not capability, is where enterprise AI budget leaks — favors platform and catalog vendors that make work discoverable over point AI tools.
insights.locator: Are AI governance and compliance slowing enterprise adoption?

insights.claim: DORA and other European Union regulations are an active blocker on AI initiatives at a Dutch health insurer, which counts as a financial institution and so faces heavy regulation on top of healthcare-specific compliance.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Names a specific regulatory instrument gating AI spend in EU financial services — vendors that pre-solve DORA compliance unlock budget faster than those adding model capability.
insights.locator: Are AI governance and compliance slowing enterprise adoption?

insights.claim: A useful architectural discipline is asking whether a problem needs AI at all: translating foreign declarations or invoices was already solved by existing input management, so applying AI to it adds cost without value even though the business is demanding AI.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A concrete filter for spotting AI-mandate-driven waste inside enterprises, and a caution when underwriting AI adoption metrics as evidence of value.
insights.locator: if you look overall, they're doing the same thing

insights.claim: Classic ML teams using Databricks with self-hosted language models are bypassing centralized services like Azure AI Foundry or AWS Bedrock, creating a governance fragmentation problem where generative AI and traditional ML follow incompatible architectural paths.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Self-hosting inside data platforms is a real leakage path away from hyperscaler managed AI services — a competitive threat to Bedrock/Foundry attach rates.
insights.locator: because the classic ML people are doing is different

insights.claim: Enterprise focus has moved in under a year from personal productivity to team-level productivity from AI, with the remaining hard problems sitting at the enterprise level.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: The buying unit is shifting from individual seat licenses to team and enterprise platforms — a repricing opportunity and a threat to per-seat AI tool vendors.
insights.locator: there is huge improvement from AI at individual level to AI at team level

insights.claim: Limiting how much MCP tool surface is exposed has become a standard enterprise compliance check, with companies explicitly ruling that not every tool can be open to everyone.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Tool-surface minimization is now a procurement checkbox — a concrete product requirement for anyone selling MCP servers into enterprises.
insights.locator: plus security in terms of how much of MCP you would be exposing

insights.claim: Despite a crazy amount of AI coding tools, consolidation has begun around Claude, Cursor and Codex, with most companies now leaning toward two or three combinations of these.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: A named shortlist forming at the enterprise tier means the AI coding tool market is consolidating faster than the funding activity implies — bad for long-tail entrants.
insights.locator: some consolidation around the Claude or Cursor or Codex

insights.claim: Developers hooking AI to internal systems through MCP inherit the permissions of whoever set them up, causing governance and compliance strife that remains largely unsolved and that materially suppressed MCP adoption until a centralized auth plugin arrived.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific technical blocker that capped MCP enterprise deployment; its removal is the trigger for expecting an adoption step-up.
insights.quote: I have perception of MCP coming in and just running roughshod over permissions and IAM that you have in your internal organization. And that inevitably has led to it not being as adopted as much as it might have been.
insights.locator: Matt, I'd love to get your thoughts on this kind of stuff

insights.claim: The right sequencing for agent governance is to bake authentication, authorization, compliance and security into the API layer first, then layer portals, MCP, ServiceNow or Jira on top — because Kubernetes-style RBAC through portals does not carry over to MCP.
insights.speaker: Daniel Bryant
insights.so_what: API-layer-first governance is the reusable architecture prescription for agent security, and it favors incumbent API management vendors over new agent-specific control planes.
insights.locator: Jim and Andrea did a fantastic talk at QCon London

insights.claim: Enterprises are shifting demand toward unglamorous enterprise-grade tooling that solves real problems rather than yet another model that ships data to an unwanted jurisdiction, which is expected to take early-adopter compliance and governance pain off the table.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Points the spend toward boring governance infrastructure rather than model access — a rotation to watch in enterprise AI budgets.
insights.quote: The uncool enterprise level tooling that isn't yet another model that's going to send all of your data to a country you don't want it to go to
insights.locator: The uncool enterprise level tooling

themes.theme: Managed AI layers as an on-ramp, not a destination

insights.claim: Managed AI platforms like AWS Bedrock are seeing a huge first-wave intake because they tick compliance and security boxes easily, but unlike a managed database they do not solve a fundamental problem, so teams will likely use them as a quick start and then move off once they see the cloud bill.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A directly bearish read on the durability of hyperscaler managed AI revenue — track Bedrock-class retention rather than initial adoption.
insights.quote: I'm quite skeptical about platform like Bedrock and similar. I really think they have a huge intake at the moment as a first wave
insights.locator: Renato, any thoughts on the security?

insights.claim: Architects now face an explicit cost-versus-security trade-off analysis on AI services, where a piece of functionality may cost 5x more than building it in-house, making total cost of ownership the deciding architectural input.
insights.speaker: Daniel Bryant
insights.so_what: A 5x managed-service premium is the threshold at which in-house build becomes rational — the number to test when modeling AI platform gross margins.
insights.locator: you're often trading off cost and security

insights.claim: AI gateway policies provide a working mechanism for cost control today — consumption policies, per-team metrics, and routing to the appropriately sized model rather than using a frontier model for trivial tasks.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Model routing at the gateway is the one AI cost lever that already works — near-term demand driver for API management vendors extending into AI.
insights.quote: so you're not using a Formula 1 car to do your groceries
insights.locator: Steef-Jan, you got any thoughts on this one as well?

themes.theme: Tokenmaxxing and the productivity measurement void

insights.claim: FinOps tools can itemize exactly how many dollars an individual developer spent on tokens across Opus, Fable and Sonnet, but none can relate that spend back to outcomes, leaving enterprises unable to justify AI budgets on value.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: The single clearest unmet need in FinOps tooling — the first credible spend-to-outcome attribution product owns the category.
insights.quote: the FinOps tools can tell you that Matt Saunders spent X, Y, Z dollars on tokens in Opus, in Fable, in Sonnet, et cetera. But none of them that I know of can actually relate that back to outcomes
insights.locator: How important is FinOps today?

insights.claim: Token spend is becoming a presenteeism proxy — engineers 'tokenmaxxing' to appear productive — after a couple of years when using AI tools felt like a guilty secret delivering outsized productivity for small spend, and the zeitgeist has now flipped to tokens being expensive.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: If token consumption is being gamed as a productivity signal, usage-based AI revenue growth partly reflects performative spend that will compress once measurement tightens.
insights.locator: it's almost like a presenteeism thing

insights.claim: The productivity measurement vacuum has revived discredited metrics like lines of code written, abandoned five years ago, because organizations lack any better way to measure AI-era output — with DORA primitives such as lead time to production offered as the more defensible fallback.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of measurement-theater in AI ROI reporting; DORA-style delivery metrics are the more credible basis for evaluating claimed AI productivity gains.
insights.locator: starting to dismantle these ideas of things like number of lines of code

insights.claim: Shining a light on AI costs creates instinctive pressure to reduce them without justification, an unsolved organizational failure mode that risks cutting spend that is actually productive.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Warns that AI cost visibility without value attribution produces indiscriminate cuts — a demand risk for AI vendors once FinOps visibility arrives before ROI measurement does.
insights.locator: just as soon as you start shining a light on costs

insights.claim: Cloud cost control has regressed from deterministic tooling — optimizing storage class, data transfer and CPU — to using a FinOps agent to manage AI spending and hoping for the best, because AI and agent-based managed services offer no full cost visibility.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Non-deterministic cost control is a structural downgrade in financial governance — a real operational risk for companies scaling agent workloads.
insights.quote: you use a FinOps agent to control your AI spending or hoping for the best
insights.locator: Renato, going to throw over to you

insights.claim: The dominant uncertainty in AI cost planning is whether current prices are subsidized by the big providers to create lock-in or reflect real long-term costs, an unknown so large it makes every other FinOps concern feel comparatively minor.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A latent repricing risk under every enterprise AI TCO model — the scenario that would invalidate current AI ROI cases wholesale.
insights.quote: are those costs subsidized right now by the big provider to lock you in or are the real costs that I'm going to sustain long term?
insights.locator: As well, the elephant in the room

insights.claim: The big rocks of AI and cloud waste have already been addressed and the next challenge is a long tail of many small agents whose aggregation cost — the effort to gather and make sense of them — exceeds the value of any individual one, which is why the FinOps Foundation spun out a Tokenomics Foundation.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Cost leakage is migrating from a few large line items to thousands of small ones, favoring attribution and observability tooling over rate negotiation.
insights.quote: instead of those big models, big investments, MLOps, et cetera, we have now reached to these small, lots of pebbles around
insights.locator: Shweta, you got any thoughts on this one?

insights.claim: There is an unresolved tension in cloud billing, invoking Corey Quinn's framing: providers have made bills so complicated that FinOps agents are now needed to parse them, when the complexity could have been avoided in the first place.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Billing complexity is a deliberate margin-protection mechanism, not an accident — relevant to assessing how durable cloud gross margins are under FinOps pressure.
insights.locator: But clouds, as usual, are difficult

insights.claim: FinOps data in enterprises typically sits between finance departments and asset owners and is not visible to engineering teams who do care, creating an information gap precisely when a small model change can 10x costs — a risk that did not exist before.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: 10x cost sensitivity to a single model swap makes engineer-facing cost visibility a new operational requirement, not a finance nicety.
insights.quote: a small change in a model could 10X your costs, whereas we didn't have that problem before
insights.locator: Mark, you got any thoughts on this one?

insights.claim: GitHub's model change on 1 June, including changes to what Pro tier power provided, was a concrete instance where engineers directly felt AI pricing decisions.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: A dated example of AI vendor repricing hitting end users — evidence that subscription AI tiers are not stable inputs for engineering cost planning.
insights.locator: I saw that firsthand on the 1st of June

themes.theme: Platform engineering in a holding pattern, agentic aside

insights.claim: Platform engineering's non-AI work is in a holding pattern: teams no longer debate how to Terraform infrastructure, where to host wiki pages, or GitHub uptime, and instead argue about data sovereignty, model hosting and access control around frontier models.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Infrastructure-as-code tooling is a mature low-growth market; platform-team growth budget has rotated entirely to model hosting and access control.
insights.quote: We're not talking about how best to Terraform stuff out or where to host your WikiPages or if GitHub is up or down anymore. It's all about data sovereignty. It's about hosting models.
insights.locator: How is platform engineering evolving in the AI era?

insights.claim: In the agentic space platform teams learn about new developments at the same time as developers, so they structurally cannot get ahead — a return to the early days of platform engineering rather than a failure.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Central platform teams have no information advantage in agentic AI, which guarantees continued shadow platform proliferation and favors bottom-up tool adoption.
insights.locator: especially in the agentic world where the platform team is finding out

insights.claim: Platform engineering teams' main mandate has become acting as AI-native enablers who avoid becoming a bottleneck and do it cost-effectively, because when the central platform is not good enough teams build their own in a completely different way.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Shadow platform emergence is the measurable failure signal for central platform investment — a practical diagnostic for whether that spend is working.
insights.locator: Mark, going across to you, do you have any experiences of the IDPs

insights.claim: At KubeCon, with over 1,500 registered and at least 1,000 in the room, roughly 70% of hands went up for platform engineering being just a rename of DevOps, indicating the discipline is still immature in perception.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: A 70% perception gap at the industry's flagship conference means category definition, not features, is still the competitive battleground for platform vendors.
insights.locator: This year when I went for KubeCon

insights.claim: Platform engineering merits an early-majority classification because the debates about one IaC vendor or Kubernetes-as-a-Service variants like PKS have ended, and because teams that start on serverless Lambdas find so much assembly required that they fall back to Kubernetes, whose services and engines have matured.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Serverless-to-Kubernetes fallback is a notable directional signal against the serverless-eats-everything thesis at enterprise scale.
insights.locator: But if I look at my own experience, I would put it in early majority

insights.claim: The internal developer portal space has matured with organizations settling on Backstage or vendor portals, while agentic developer portals built around skills, plugins and hooks are at the equivalent of IDPs' earliest days but are expected to mature faster.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Agentic developer portals are the next tooling wave; a compressed maturation window means entrants have less time to establish position than IDP vendors did.
insights.locator: And quickly on the Agentic developer portals

insights.claim: The platform engineer and developer roles must now formally diverge by abstraction layer, with developers working at higher abstractions while platform engineers stay grounded in infrastructure and Kubernetes — a distinction being actively taught to teams to make user experience tractable.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Role separation by abstraction layer is the organizational prerequisite for platform investment paying off — a diligence question for engineering-org assessment.
insights.quote: there has to be a difference between a platform engineer and a developer now
insights.locator: my next statement might surprise you

insights.claim: A Dutch health insurer's applications, systems, hyperscalers and even its Oracle-based policy system are all American, so achieving full sovereignty would require rebuilding and re-engineering everything — making sovereignty architecturally infeasible in practice.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sovereignty demand converts to migration slowly and partially; expect IaaS-layer wins rather than full-stack displacement of US vendors.
insights.locator: How are organisations approaching digital sovereignty?

insights.claim: European cloud providers can supply IaaS and storage but the platform and SaaS layers are far harder, with no obvious sovereign alternative to Salesforce as a CRM where heavy investment has already been made.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: US SaaS incumbents face materially less sovereignty displacement risk than US IaaS — the layer distinction that matters for sizing the threat.
insights.locator: The European cloud providers can provide IaaS

insights.claim: All of one Birmingham-based consultancy's clients are European and adamant about keeping everything within Europe, with about half gradually migrating back on-premises as a clear observed trend.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Sovereignty-driven repatriation is real at the mid-market regulated tier — a narrow but genuine headwind to hyperscaler European growth and a tailwind for on-prem infrastructure.
insights.quote: about half of our clients are actually gradually migrating back on-prem. It's absolutely a trend that I've seen.
insights.locator: Mark, can I go to you on this?

insights.claim: The sovereignty objection resembles the earlier banks-can't-move-to-the-cloud objection that cloud providers eventually solved, and the panic-driven response of vibecoding replacement services to run under a desk is already receding as the political climate improves and vendors address the problem.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A mean-reversion view: sovereignty is a solvable vendor-feature problem rather than a permanent structural break — the bear case against sovereign-cloud challenger investments.
insights.locator: Matt, have you got any thoughts on this one?

insights.claim: Most European cloud alternatives are mostly marketing and do not provide services at the level required to be a real alternative, echoing the early S3 era when a claimed S3 backend was a single server with an S3 API and none of the scalability.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Directly bearish on European sovereign-cloud challengers as investments — regulatory tailwind is not matched by delivered capability.
insights.quote: It reminds me a bit the early day of S3 when everyone was claiming to have a S3 backend that was basically just one single server running with a S3 API.
insights.locator: Renato, you got any thoughts now?

insights.claim: The main positive effect of hyperscalers launching European regions has been to make teams aware of a jurisdictional challenge they had not previously considered when deploying to standard European regions, even though whether those regions are truly European is contested.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Awareness, not capability, is the near-term product of the sovereign-region push — meaning demand is being created faster than supply can satisfy it.
insights.locator: even the fact that the cloud provider themselves provide now new regions

insights.claim: Sovereignty for models is conceptually incoherent because models are trained on internet data that is already everybody's data and already shared, so it is unclear whether the boundary being secured is data or model — and if models, it may be too late to secure at all.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Undermines the technical basis for model-level sovereignty offerings from AWS, GCP and Azure — a reason to discount sovereign-AI marketing claims.
insights.locator: Shweta, any final thoughts on this topic?

insights.claim: The narrative that AI will kill the junior or senior engineer role is dying down, as are radical predictions of how different the world will look in 5, 10 or 15 years.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A sentiment reversal among practitioners against the AI-displaces-developers thesis — relevant to positioning in dev tooling and technical staffing.
insights.locator: Which cloud and DevOps trends are overrated?

insights.claim: Fully autonomous agents in enterprise environments are overrated for now because humans must remain in the loop, and in regulated settings like health insurance decision-making must always be a human or a doctor.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: A regulatory ceiling on autonomy caps the automatable share of workflows in insurance and healthcare regardless of model capability.
insights.locator: Mark, up to you

insights.claim: The move from microservices to an agentic world is qualitatively harder because microservices were predictable like taxis running A to B, whereas agentic systems are not — so teams should focus on agentic harnesses and meshes rather than sophisticated portals, skills and surface features.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: A due-diligence filter favoring vendors solving mesh and harness plumbing over those selling agent UI surfaces.
insights.locator: Shweta, what do you think?

insights.claim: AWS has killed and renamed its services thousands of times in the past year, and at least two or three of the major managed AI services will disappear in the next 12 months as developers come to care less about which model runs behind an assistant and more about what it does.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable call on hyperscaler AI SKU rationalization, plus the thesis that model identity is commoditizing into an implementation detail.
insights.quote: I will bet at least two, three of the major one will disappear in the next 12 months, and developer will start to care less about which models is running behind them
insights.locator: Renato, over to you

insights.claim: Agent washing — vendors claiming agents can do everything — mirrors the earlier DevOps veneer era where buyers purchased all new tools that were the same tools rebranded, and the discipline is to ask what value the AI in a platform or SaaS product actually adds when the task is often better covered by an existing service.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A vendor-evaluation heuristic drawn from a repeat historical pattern — expect a meaningful share of AI-labelled product revenue to be rebranding rather than new capability.
insights.locator: Steef-Jan?
